title: THC Vape Buying Guide: Carts, Disposables and Oils
h1: How to Buy a THC Vape: Hardware, Oil Type and Potency

body:
A THC vape buying guide really comes down to four decisions: the hardware you want, the type of oil inside, how strong you want it, and whether it fits the battery you own. Make them in that order and the vape shelf gets a lot less confusing. Here’s how to work through each one, which mistakes to skip, and the care that keeps a cart working.

## THC vape buying guide: the four decisions

1. **Hardware.** An all-in-one disposable, or a cartridge you screw onto a rechargeable battery.
2. **Oil type.** Distillate, live resin or live rosin, each made a different way.
3. **Potency.** The THC content of the oil, and how that fits your experience.
4. **Compatibility.** Whether a cart fits your battery, or a pod fits its device.

Settle the first one and the other three narrow quickly.

## Disposable or cartridge: who each suits

A disposable is a battery and oil in one sealed device. You use it until the oil runs out, then recycle it. There’s no battery to match, and some models don’t need charging at all, which makes a disposable an easy first vape or a handy backup. Our guide to [disposable vapes](/blog/cannabis-disposable-vapes/) goes deeper.

A cartridge, or cart, holds the oil and screws onto a separate battery. Buy the battery once, and after that you’re only buying carts. You can switch strains and oil types freely, and many batteries let you choose a heat setting.

A disposable probably suits you if you vape now and then, want nothing to set up, or are new to vaping. A cart and battery probably suit you if you vape regularly, like switching between strains, or want control over the heat.

### Side by side

| | Disposable | Cartridge and battery |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | None: open it and use it | Screw the cart onto a charged battery |
| Upkeep | Little; some models recharge | Charge the battery and keep the threads clean |
| Variety | Whatever comes in the device | Any cart that fits your battery |
| Heat control | Usually fixed | Often adjustable |
| Cost over time | Every device includes a new battery | The battery is a one-time cost, so refills usually cost less |
| Good fit for | First-timers, travel days, occasional use | Regular use and trying different oils |

## Oil types: distillate vs live resin vs live rosin

The oil matters as much as the hardware. Vape concentrates are far stronger than flower: a 2025 review put THC in commercial concentrates at more than 50% and up to about 95%, against roughly 10% to 30% in plant material. How the oil is made shapes what comes along with that THC.

### Distillate

Distillate is THC refined until little else is left, then usually blended with terpenes for flavor. Its taste depends on what was added back, and since it is mostly THC, its THC number tends to run high.

### Live resin

Live resin is extracted from plants frozen right after harvest instead of dried and cured, usually with hydrocarbon solvents in a licensed lab. Freezing skips the drying step, which can cost cannabis some of its aroma compounds, so live resin aims to keep more of the plant’s own terpenes and taste closer to the original strain.

### Live rosin

Live rosin starts with the same fresh-frozen plants but uses no solvents. The plants are washed in ice water to collect the resin glands, and that hash is pressed with heat. For a closer comparison, see [live resin vs live rosin](/blog/live-resin-vs-live-rosin/).

### Buy licensed, and don’t add anything

In 2019 and early 2020, a national outbreak of lung injuries among people who vaped was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate, an additive found in some THC vape products. Most patients who said where their THC products came from reported informal sources only, like friends or dealers. CDC and FDA advised people not to use THC vaping products, especially from those sources, and not to add anything to a vape product.

A licensed Michigan store sells tested, labeled products. That doesn’t make vaping harmless: a 2025 review found that heating cannabis concentrates can release harmful compounds, and research on the health risks of vaping them lags far behind how widely these products are used.

## Potency: why THC percentage isn’t everything

Vape oil is strong by design, so the useful question isn’t which cart has the highest number. It’s how much THC you take in, and you control that mostly through the length and number of your pulls.

- **Read the whole label,** not just the THC number. The list below shows what a Michigan cart label includes.
- **A higher number means a stronger pull,** not better flavor or a better time.
- **Terpenes shape flavor and aroma.** Two carts with similar THC can taste quite different. Our guide to [terpenes in vape oil](/blog/terpenes-in-thc-vape-oil/) explains why.
- **Shop by tier, not by maximum.** If you want something lighter, look for a lower THC number, such as a cart that blends THC with CBD. If you’re experienced, a standard-strength cart taken in small pulls may suit you better than the strongest option.

Inhaled THC acts fast: effects begin within minutes and reach their height in about 15 to 30 minutes, according to a pharmacology review. Start with one short pull and wait before deciding on another.

### What a Michigan cart label shows

Every licensed product carries a label, and a vape cart’s is worth a slow read:

- THC and CBD content, with a note that actual values may vary by 10%
- The strain, where one applies
- The testing lab and the test date
- Net weight, so you can compare cart sizes
- Michigan’s universal THC symbol and the required warnings

## Hardware fit: 510 thread or pods

Most standard carts use a 510 thread, the common screw-in connection, so carts and batteries from different makers usually fit together. A few details still matter:

- **Width and shape.** A wide cart may not sit flush in a battery with a sleeve or a recessed top.
- **Draw style.** Some batteries fire when you inhale; others use a button. Both work with 510 carts.
- **Heat settings.** A variable battery lets you start low, which is gentler on the oil and its flavor.

Pod systems work differently. A pod is made for one specific device and fits only that device, so the pod and the battery have to come from the same system. Before you buy pods, make sure you have, or want, the matching battery.

### Battery basics

If you’re buying a 510 battery, three features are worth looking for. Adjustable heat settings let you start low and step up only if you need to. A preheat function gently warms thick oil, which helps on cold Michigan mornings. And a battery with a charge indicator spares you a dead pen halfway through the day.

## Common vape-buying mistakes

- **Mismatched hardware.** A pod won’t work on a 510 battery, and a wide cart can wobble in a narrow one.
- **Shopping by THC alone.** The biggest number tells you strength, not flavor or whether you’ll enjoy it.
- **Ignoring oil type.** If flavor matters to you, so does the gap between distillate and live products.
- **Buying on price alone.** A bargain battery that runs hot can scorch a good cart, and a cart from outside a licensed store isn’t worth the savings.
- **Skipping the label.** Check the THC content, the oil type and the testing lab before you leave.

## Care basics that protect your purchase

- **Store carts upright,** mouthpiece on top, so oil stays where the heating element can reach it.
- **Keep it out of heat and sun.** FDA advises keeping vapes out of direct sunlight and out of a car on a hot day. Michigan winters bring the opposite problem: cold thickens oil, so let a cart warm up before you use it.
- **Pull slowly and gently.** Hard, fast draws can drag oil into the airway and clog it.
- **Charge with care.** Use the charger made for your battery, not a phone or tablet charger, and don’t charge it overnight, both FDA tips.
- **Recycle batteries properly.** Lithium-ion batteries, including the ones inside disposables, don’t belong in household trash or curbside recycling bins. Take them to a battery recycling or household hazardous waste drop-off.

If a cart clogs or leaks anyway, our guide to [fixing clogged and leaking vapes](/blog/vape-care-prevent-clogs-leaks/) walks through the fixes.

## Matching a vape to how you shop

Put the four decisions together and most people land in one of a few places:

- **Trying vaping for the first time:** a disposable, or a battery on its lowest setting with a distillate cart, and short pulls.
- **Flavor first:** a live resin or live rosin cart on a battery with adjustable heat, kept on a low setting.
- **Regular use on a budget:** one good 510 battery and refill carts, which usually beats buying disposables over time.
- **Quick stops:** know your format and oil type before you go, or order ahead.

Vape pens and carts are a regular part of High Society’s menus, though selection varies by store and changes often. Browse your store’s [online menu](/shop/), order ahead for in-store or curbside pickup, and if you choose curbside, we’ll text you when your order is ready. Our budtenders can help you match a cart to your battery, and current promotions are on our [deals page](/deals/). Bring a valid government-issued ID: recreational shopping is for adults 21 and older, and medical patients 18 and older with a valid card are welcome too. Enjoy responsibly.

faq.q: Cartridge or disposable: which costs less over time?
faq.a: For regular use, a cartridge on a rechargeable battery usually does. You buy the battery once and then pay only for carts, while every disposable comes with a new battery built in. For occasional use, a disposable can still make sense, since there’s nothing else to buy or keep charged.

faq.q: Does live resin hit harder than distillate?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Distillate can carry the higher THC number because it’s refined THC, while live resin’s appeal is flavor and more of the plant’s own terpenes. How strong a pull feels depends on the THC content, your heat setting and how deeply you inhale, so compare the numbers rather than the oil type alone.

faq.q: How do I know a battery fits my cart?
faq.a: Check the connection first. Most standard carts and batteries use a 510 thread, so they usually screw together across brands. Then check the cart’s width against any sleeve or recess on the battery. Pods are the exception: they fit only the device they were made for. When in doubt, bring both to a budtender.

A disposable, or a simple battery on its lowest setting with a modest-strength cart. Take one short, gentle pull, wait several minutes, and decide from there. Inhaled THC comes on much faster than an edible, so it’s easier to stop where you are. Our budtenders are happy to talk through options.

faq.q: How long does a disposable usually last?
faq.a: There’s no single answer: the amount of oil, how often you vape and how long your pulls are all play a part. A disposable that sits unused for a long time can also lose charge or thicken. Check the oil volume on the package and keep track of how long one lasts you.
